channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Power
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] UK confirms a cyber incident at a small generator — an asset sitting below the regulated reporting threshold
item.description: The UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has confirmed on the record that a cyber incident affected a small-scale energy generator, stating that at no point was the wider energy system at risk. It is the first publicly acknowledged cyberattack on a British generating asset. The headline claims — four days offline, attribution to Iran, the word unprecedented — come from unnamed officials via the Sunday Telegraph on 22 August, and the NCSC declined to comment. No plant, operator, technology or access route has been published, so there is no vector to defend against yet. The detail that matters operationally is that the NCSC logged no outage reports from regulated power station operators. That places the affected site beneath the reporting regime — and Britain’s embedded generation, CHP, standby and storage estate is numerous, often unmanned, and commonly reached through vendor remote access. - Sunday Telegraph report, with on-record statement from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero — via Irish Times, CNBC, Security Affairs - Telegraph report 22 Aug 2026; DESNZ statement and international pickup 23 Aug 2026; attack reported as occurring in July 2026, exact date not published

item.title: [Critical] Treasury names an Iranian intelligence-directed hacking network that has been inside US energy companies since 2023
item.category: Incident — Nation-state targeting of energy companies
item.description: The US Treasury designated an Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security–directed hacking group on 24 August, as part of a wider action covering nearly 60 Iran-linked people, entities and vessels. Treasury states the network has breached and exfiltrated data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023; five alleged operators, described as tied to the Mabna Institute, were indicted by the Justice Department the preceding week. Read the scope carefully, because it is the part that matters for a utility risk register. What is attributed here is espionage and data theft — engineering drawings, network documentation, credentials and personnel records — not manipulation of generation or transmission equipment. The separate campaign that has degraded water-utility operations through internet-facing controllers remains formally unattributed by CISA. Two clusters, one adversary, only one of them named. The reason a generation or transmission operator should care is that access collected for espionage converts to disruption when tasking changes: the credentials, vendor footholds and remote-management paths this group is described as using are the same ones a disruptive operator would inherit. The State Department has posted a $10 million reward on related activity. - US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; Department of Justice indictment; State Department Rewards for Justice notice — via The Hacker News, CyberScoop and Nextgov/FCW - Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; DOJ indictments the preceding week; trade-press analysis 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Five federal agencies warn AI-written scripts are reading Siemens S7 controllers across the energy sector
item.description: The NSA, CISA, FBI, Department of Energy and EPA issued a joint advisory on 19 August warning that threat actors are combining the open-source snap7 and python-snap7 automation libraries with AI-assisted scripting to build tools that mimic legitimate OT monitoring software. Those tools give read and write access to Siemens S7 controller memory, configuration data and ladder logic over S7comm. Energy is named among the most-targeted sectors, alongside critical manufacturing, water, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities. The agencies say actors locate exposed devices with internet scanning services and get in through default or weak credentials rather than any vulnerability. Affected lines run from the legacy S7-200 and S7-300 through the S7-1200 and S7-1500, including F-series safety controllers. The agencies assess the activity as positioning for later disruptive write operations. - Joint advisory AA26-231A (NSA, CISA, FBI, DOE, EPA) — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Help Net Security - Issued 19 Aug 2026; reported 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Attackers crossed from a wind farm into an unrelated Polish CHP plant over a shared private cellular APN
item.description: CERT Polska disclosed on 9 August, at DEF CON, that attackers reached the industrial control network of a Polish combined heat and power plant serving roughly 50,000 residents by pivoting through a private cellular data network. The intrusion began somewhere else entirely: an internet-exposed Fortinet VPN and firewall device at a wind farm on the same carrier APN. Because the APN was misconfigured to let arbitrary devices address one another, the attacker crossed from one generator’s network into another operator’s controllers. CERT Polska describes this as the first observed real-world use of a private APN as a route into an OT network. The incident occurred on 29 December 2025, the same day as coordinated attacks on 30 Polish renewable facilities and another CHP plant; ESET attributes that operation to the Russia-aligned Sandworm group with medium confidence. Analysis of the smaller plant took more than three months, which is why it was omitted from the original report. - CERT Polska disclosure — reported by SecurityWeek, Help Net Security and BleepingComputer - Incident 29 Dec 2025; disclosed 9 Aug 2026, analysis published 10–11 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Clop has named more than 40 victims of a PTC Windchill campaign, and what it took is engineering data
item.description: The Clop extortion group has listed over 40 organisations on its leak site following a mass data-theft campaign against internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM product lifecycle management instances, exploiting CVE-2026-12569, an improper input validation flaw allowing arbitrary code execution. Named organisations include Shell, Philips, Fiserv, Zebra, Mindray and Largan Precision. Researchers report the affiliates deployed JSP web shells to exfiltrate data, with activity going back to early June, and confirmed victims spanning manufacturing, automotive, aerospace and retail. For a generation or transmission operator the exposure is rarely the plant floor — it is the design record. Single-line diagrams, protection settings, factory acceptance test reports and vendor configuration files held in a PLM or engineering document system are exactly the material that makes a later, targeted intrusion cheaper for someone else. - Clop leak-site listings — reported by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Listings reported 15 Aug 2026; campaign since early Jun 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s red team crossed a utility-style domain undetected — through Active Directory defaults, not exotic tooling
item.description: CISA published AA26-237A on 25 August comparing two red-team assessments run with near-identical tradecraft: one against a government services and facilities organisation, one against a water and wastewater systems entity. Both engagements opened with phishing and then escalated through Active Directory weaknesses that are ordinary rather than clever — a default Machine Account Quota still set at 10, and misconfigured Active Directory Certificate Services templates. The outcomes diverged sharply, and the divergence is the lesson. At the organisation CISA labels A, the team obtained elevated domain privileges and reached sensitive business systems and cloud resources without ever being caught, despite the organisation running multiple security operations centres and multiple EDR products. CISA’s stated reason deserves reading twice: the SOCs did not talk to each other, and thousands of false positives generated by routine business activity buried the signal. For a utility, the corporate Active Directory that this tradecraft targets is very often the same directory that authenticates engineering workstations, historians and the EMS support estate — which makes a domain compromise an OT problem one trust relationship later. - CISA cybersecurity advisory AA26-237A — joint red-team assessment findings - Published 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Six agencies warn the Gunra ransomware crew is walking into critical infrastructure through two 2025 Fortinet bugs
item.description: CISA, the FBI, the Defense Cyber Crime Center, the NSA, the Secret Service and the Korean National Police Agency published joint advisory AA26-222A on 10 August on Gunra, a ransomware operation that has hit organisations across critical infrastructure sectors since April 2025. The advisory’s operational point is unglamorous: Gunra’s initial access is overwhelmingly through internet-facing edge devices, and specifically two Fortinet flaws — CVE-2024-21762 and CVE-2024-55591 — both patched in 2025 and both still reachable on unpatched appliances. Once inside, the group steals data before encrypting, and runs a double-extortion leak site. The agencies published detection guidance, indicators and a set of mitigations centred on patching edge appliances, enforcing phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication and segmenting recovery infrastructure. For power operators the relevance is the access path rather than the ransomware. Fortinet appliances sit in front of a great many substation aggregation links, generation site DMZs and third-party maintenance connections, and the two CVEs Gunra relies on were fixed more than a year ago — meaning any operator still exposed is exposed to a documented, agency-confirmed campaign rather than a theoretical one. - CISA / FBI / DC3 / NSA / USSS / ROK National Police joint advisory AA26-222A — reported by The Record and Infosecurity Magazine - Published 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] Industrial ransomware rose 12 percent in Q2 and did not need control-system access to stop output
item.description: Dragos recorded 1,140 ransomware incidents involving industrial organisations in the second quarter of 2026, up from 1,020 in the first. Manufacturing absorbed 747 of them, roughly 65 percent, with construction at 176, equipment manufacturing at 114 and food and beverage at 70. The headline finding for operators is about mechanism rather than volume: disrupting the IT systems that support an industrial environment is frequently enough to interrupt production even when the operators never reach the control system. Extortion also continued shifting away from file encryption toward data theft, which changes what a tabletop exercise needs to rehearse. For utilities the parallel systems are outage and work management, GIS, metering and settlement — all of which can halt field work and customer operations without a single relay being touched. - Dragos Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis — via Help Net Security - Published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Low] Justice Department charges 17 people over an IRGC-linked intellectual property theft campaign
item.description: Federal prosecutors announced charges on 18 August against 17 people alleged to be members and affiliates of the Iran-based Mabna Institute, over a long-running data-theft operation said to have been run for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and other Iranian government and university clients. The 14-count superseding indictment adds eight defendants to a case first brought against nine others in 2018. Prosecutors allege intrusions at 144 US universities, 42 private companies and at least five federal and state agencies since 2013, with roughly 31.5 terabytes of academic and intellectual property material taken. The activity is espionage and theft rather than control-system manipulation, and it is separate from the PLC targeting federal agencies have warned about. It is included here as context for the attribution language now attached to Iranian-affiliated activity against US critical infrastructure. - US Department of Justice press release — corroborated by Cybersecurity Dive and Nextgov/FCW - Indictment unsealed 18 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] A conferencing server was made to hand out a backdoored client to the engineers who joined the call
item.category: Threat intel — Supply chain / engineering workstations
item.description: Kaspersky ICS-CERT reported on 12 August that the Head Mare group chained two flaws in unpatched TrueConf Server installations — tracked by Kaspersky as KLCERT-26-057 and KLCERT-26-058 — to run code and escalate privileges on the server, then swapped the legitimate client installer for a trojanised build carrying the PhantomCore and PhantomGraph backdoors. Anyone who subsequently updated their conferencing client from that server was infected. The victims named span instrumentation, electronics, transportation, energy, IT and software development. TrueConf shipped fixes on 18 June 2026 for versions 5.3.x before 5.3.9, 5.4.x before 5.4.9 and 5.5.x before 5.5.5; the exploited servers were simply never updated. Utilities are a named target set here — Kaspersky lists energy among the sectors hit. Conferencing servers are almost never in the OT asset register, yet the engineers who join those calls are the same people whose laptops hold relay configuration tools, EMS client software and substation VPN profiles. A trojanised client pushed as a routine update lands directly on the engineering desktop, which is exactly the foothold a grid intruder wants. - Kaspersky ICS-CERT — corroborated by The Hacker News and SC Media - Published 12 Aug 2026; patches released 18 Jun 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA sets a three-day federal deadline on a CVSS 10.0 Oracle web-tier flaw now under active attack
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-21962 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 24 August with a remediation date of 27 August — the tightest window Binding Operational Directive 26-04 permits. The flaw is an improper access control issue in Oracle HTTP Server and in the Oracle WebLogic Server Proxy Plug-in for Apache HTTP Server and Microsoft IIS, carrying a CVSS score of 10.0. It is reachable over HTTP by an unauthenticated attacker with no user interaction and no existing privileges, and successful exploitation allows access to the instance or modification of the data it fronts. Oracle issued the fix in its January 2026 critical patch update; reporting on 25 August describes broad exploitation against WebLogic servers. A three-day federal deadline is the signal worth reading — CISA reserves that window for exploitation it assesses as both live and consequential. This is not an ICS product and it is not on your plant floor, but Oracle’s web tier is a very common reverse proxy in front of utility enterprise applications: outage management portals, work management, asset management, customer systems and the reporting layers that pull from the historian. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition; Oracle critical patch update — corroborated by SecurityWeek and The Hacker News - Added to KEV 24 Aug 2026; federal remediation deadline 27 Aug 2026; Oracle fix issued Jan 2026; broad exploitation reported 25 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Citrix is telling admins to patch NetScaler now — an unauthenticated bypass on the appliance that fronts most OT remote access
item.description: Citrix published bulletin CTX696939 on 20 August covering two NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway flaws. The serious one, CVE-2026-19490, is an authentication bypass carrying a CVSS score of 9.3: on Gateway and AAA virtual-server configurations an unauthenticated attacker can skip the login step entirely. The second, CVE-2026-19489, is a memory overflow that can produce unpredictable behaviour or a denial of service, and only applies where SIP ALG is enabled on a Large Scale NAT group. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.32 and 13.1-63.21 or later. Citrix, Rapid7 and Finland’s national cyber authority all said they were not aware of in-the-wild exploitation at publication, while urging immediate patching — NetScaler has a long record of exploited edge flaws. For a utility this is the appliance that fronts vendor and engineering access into EMS, SCADA and substation networks, and increasingly the one carrying operator access into DER and storage fleets. An authentication bypass there is not an IT problem — it is a door into the control-centre perimeter that does not need a stolen credential. - Citrix security bulletin CTX696939 — reported by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News - Bulletin published 20 Aug 2026; reported 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Fire-alarm management software stores its credentials in cleartext in memory, CISA warns
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-232-01 on 20 August covering Johnson Controls Simplex Incident Manager, the software operators use to monitor and manage Simplex fire alarm panels across a property portfolio. Versions up to and including V2.01 keep user passwords and authentication tokens unencrypted in system memory while the application runs, tracked as CVE-2026-27875 and classified as CWE-316. A local attacker who already holds low-privileged access to the workstation can read those credentials out of memory and reuse them against the application and the systems it connects to. CISA lists critical manufacturing, commercial facilities, government facilities, transportation systems and energy among the affected sectors, with deployment worldwide. Johnson Controls has published remediation guidance in JCI-PSA-2026-28. Generating stations, control centres and large substations run Simplex fire detection under exactly this kind of portfolio management software, and the workstation is usually treated as a facilities asset rather than a control system — often outside CIP scope, often shared, often locally administered. That is the access level this flaw needs. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-232-01; Johnson Controls product security advisory JCI-PSA-2026-28 - Published 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] August ICS Patch Tuesday: maximum-severity missing authentication in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced
item.description: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The most serious, SSA-834709, covers a maximum-severity missing authentication flaw in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with elevated privileges. Siemens also fixed a critical code execution vulnerability in Siveillance Video Management Servers, and high-severity issues in Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran, Siemens License Server, Simcenter Femap, Parasolid and Logo! Soft Comfort that can crash applications, execute code, elevate privileges or read arbitrary files. Medium-severity issues were resolved in Ruggedcom devices and Desigo controllers. Schneider Electric published two advisories covering NetBotz 5 and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, and Phoenix Contact issued one for multiple PLCnext firmware flaws. Honeywell released several advisories for its building management products. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709, Schneider Electric, Phoenix Contact and Honeywell advisories — summarised by SecurityWeek - Published 12 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco ASA and FTD VPN zero-day exploited to reload firewalls, added to CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco has patched CVE-2026-20349, a flaw in the remote-access SSL VPN service of Secure Firewall ASA and Secure Firewall Threat Defense software that attackers have been exploiting to knock appliances offline. A specially crafted HTTP request to the vulnerable service causes an unexpected reload and a denial-of-service condition; no authentication and no user interaction are required. Cisco’s PSIRT confirmed active exploitation in August, and CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of 14 August. Hot fixes cover ASA 9.16, 9.18, 9.20, 9.22, 9.23 and 9.24 and FTD 7.0, 7.2, 7.4, 7.6, 7.7 and 10.0. For utilities the concern is availability rather than data: these appliances commonly terminate vendor and engineer access into substation and control-centre networks, so an unexpected reload takes remote support with it. - Cisco security advisory and CISA KEV catalogue — reported by Help Net Security and SecurityWeek - Exploitation confirmed and KEV listed Aug 2026; reported 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Hitachi Energy APM Edge and Johnson Controls Airwall in CISA’s mid-August energy-sector batch
item.description: CISA’s advisories published in the 11 to 13 August window included three products flagged for use in the energy sector. Hitachi Energy APM Edge, advisory ICSA-26-225-04, carries CVE-2026-43284 and CVE-2026-43500 affecting versions up to and including 6.10; the flaws let a local unprivileged user escalate to root through the way the kernel handles memory pages when processing ESP-encrypted network packets, with injected code running as root. Johnson Controls Airwall, ICSA-26-225-03, has an arbitrary file read vulnerability, with Johnson Controls recommending version 4.1.0 or later across all Airwall deployments. The batch also covered ANDRITZ HIPASE-250 and 250 SCALA, protection and control platforms used in hydro and industrial generation, and Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808. None is reported as exploited, but APM Edge and Airwall both sit in asset-performance and secure-connectivity roles where local access is often assumed benign. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-225-03 and ICSA-26-225-04 — roundup via WaterISAC - Published 11–13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Four more exploited flaws added to KEV on 18 August, including Windows IKE and VMware vCenter
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August: CVE-2026-33824 in Microsoft Internet Key Exchange, CVE-2026-55040 in Microsoft SharePoint, CVE-2026-59310 in Broadcom VMware vCenter and CVE-2026-65400 in Apple macOS. Two more followed on 20 August, both in TrueConf Server. The IKE and vCenter entries are the ones that matter most in a utility context. IKE is the service terminating site-to-site tunnels between control centres, substations and vendor networks, so a flaw there sits directly on the path CIP-012 asks you to protect. vCenter is frequently the management plane for the virtualised infrastructure hosting historians, HMI servers and engineering workstations — compromise there is a hypervisor-level problem, not an application one. None of these is an ICS product, which is precisely why they tend to fall outside the OT patch cycle. - CISA KEV catalogue additions - Added 18 Aug 2026; two further additions 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] CISA publishes an advisory for flaws in Malcolm, its own free OT network monitoring suite
item.description: Advisory ICSA-26-230-01 covers vulnerabilities in Malcolm, the network traffic analysis suite CISA distributes free for OT and ICS environments. The flaws could let an attacker cause a denial-of-service condition or execute arbitrary code, and affect Malcolm versions below 26.06.1, below 26.07.0 and up to and including 26.07.1. The same day CISA published ICSA-26-230-02 covering a stack overflow in Siemens Simcenter Nastran that can be triggered when the application binary reads an arbitrary string as a file argument, with remote code execution possible if a user is tricked into running it; Siemens has released updated versions. Malcolm deserves attention out of proportion to its install base because it is often deployed by smaller utilities without a commercial OT monitoring budget, sits on a span or tap with visibility into the whole control network, and is not always in anyone’s patch inventory. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-230-01 and ICSA-26-230-02 - Published 18 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] AVEVA Enterprise SCADA can be pushed into executing code through tampered serialised data
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-01, published 13 August as part of a 15-advisory batch, covers a deserialisation flaw in AVEVA Enterprise SCADA. An attacker who already holds the “DNA Authority — Operator” privilege can tamper with serialised data and have it execute as code when the server deserialises it. The 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 release families are affected, along with certain Enterprise SCADA HMI versions. CISA reports no known public exploitation targeting this flaw. AVEVA’s guidance is to restrict operator rights to trusted users, disallow BLT test clients in production, and audit devices, network topology and perimeter defences; the vendor also points to KB117814 on removing the binary formatter. Enterprise SCADA is deployed on transmission and distribution control estates and across midstream operations, so the population here is control-room grade rather than office grade. The saving grace is the privilege requirement — but “authenticated operator” is a low bar inside a control room where shared or long-lived accounts are still common, and it is exactly the account a contractor or an intruder with a stolen VPN credential ends up holding. - CISA ICSA-26-225-01 — corroborated by AVEVA security bulletin AVEVA-2026-005 - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] The 2026 CIP picture: CIP-003-9 and CIP-012-2 in force, CIP-015 internal monitoring ahead
item.description: Two standards changed day-to-day practice this year. CIP-003-9 extends security management control expectations to low-impact BES cyber systems, with explicit attention to vendor remote access and to detecting malicious communications at low-impact assets. CIP-012-2 tightens protection of real-time operational data exchanged between control centres, including confidentiality and data handling rather than integrity and availability alone. Looking forward, CIP-015 introduces internal network security monitoring for high and medium impact BES cyber systems with external routable connectivity, and FERC has directed that its scope be extended. A further final rule approves CIP-003-11 modifications improving baseline security for low-impact systems through new password protocols for remote users and intrusion detection. The through-line is consistent: low-impact sites and vendor access are where the next audit attention lands, and internal monitoring is no longer optional at the high and medium tier. - FERC orders and NERC CIP standards — summarised by Certrec and Industrial Cyber - CIP-003-9 and CIP-012-2 effective 2026; CIP-015 scope expansion directed by FERC

item.title: [Low] US and Australian agencies publish guidance on isolating OT and running that way for an extended period
item.description: A joint publication from US and Australian agencies sets out how critical infrastructure operators should prepare to isolate vital operational technology and supporting systems from external connectivity, and to keep operating in that isolated state for an extended period rather than for the few hours most continuity plans assume. It is guidance, not a requirement, and creates no compliance obligation. The value for a utility is that it turns an assumption most operators state confidently — that they can drop to manual or islanded operation if the corporate network is compromised — into a checklist that names the dependencies people forget: time synchronisation, licence servers, authentication, historian writes, remote vendor support and the physical availability of local operating staff. The water sector incidents this summer showed several utilities reverting to manual control successfully; the ones that struggled generally discovered a dependency nobody had documented. - Joint US–Australian OT isolation guidance — reported by SecurityWeek - Published 29 Jul 2026
